level_mis_links.exact_rule: wrong rule: Making every variable a double is the right fix for integer division. Right rule: Use int for countable things and double for measured ones; where a fraction is needed, make one operand of the division a double (or cast) instead of changing every type.

wrong rule: A variable declared int can hold 2.5 or "hi"; the type is only a label. Right rule: A data type is a set of values and a set of operations defined on them, so an int variable holds only int values.

Points to LT (find each operand's type, then apply that type's operator). Applied unevenly, a student uses the int operator for 7 / 2 in one line (3) but real division in the next (3.5), or treats a String "12" as a number in one + and as text in another. (here mixing in: "Making every variable a double is the right fix for integer division")

Widening a variable's type (int to double) usually still compiles but changes which operations run: / keeps fractions and output prints 3.0. Narrowing it (double to int) breaks every assignment of a double value with a compile-time error. Values that fit both types are kept.
wrong rule: 10 / 3 evaluates to 3.333. Right rule: Dividing two ints gives an int: the fractional part is discarded.
wrong rule: An int result that is too large is automatically stored as a bigger number. Right rule: int arithmetic is 32-bit; a result outside the range wraps around.

Points to LT (each int operation is done immediately in 32-bit integer arithmetic). Applied unevenly, a student truncates 10 / 3 to 3 in one step but computes 10 / 3 * 3 as 10, or wraps on one overflow but not another. (here mixing in: "10 / 3 evaluates to 3.333")
Changing a variable from int to double changes / from truncating to fractional, and output from 3 to 3.0. Multiplying before dividing keeps precision (59 * 100 / 60 is 98, but 59 / 60 * 100 is 0).

wrong rule: System.out.Println and System.out.println name the same method. Right rule: Java is case-sensitive: names of variables, methods and classes that differ only in capitalization are different names.
wrong rule: keywords may be reused as identifiers. Right rule: Keywords are reserved by Java and cannot be used as variable names.

Points to LT (a name refers to the declaration with exactly that spelling in scope). Applied unevenly, a student treats Count and count as one variable in one statement but as two in another. (here mixing in: "System.out.Println and System.out.println name the same method")

Renaming an identifier consistently at its declaration and every use leaves behavior unchanged. Renaming only some occurrences, or changing only the capitalization, breaks compilation with 'cannot find symbol'.
wrong rule: String is a primitive type like int. Right rule: String is not a primitive type; it is a class whose values are objects, although Java gives it some built-in support (literals, +).

Points to LT (each operation is done in its type's fixed size). Applied unevenly, a student truncates and wraps int results on one line but treats another int intermediate as an unbounded real number, e.g. tracing 59 / 60 * 100 as 98. (here mixing in: "String is a primitive type like int")

wrong rule: The slots of a new int[n] hold unpredictable values until assigned. Right rule: new fills every element with a default: 0 for numeric types, false for boolean, null for String and other non-primitive types.

Switching one primitive type for another changes range and precision. int to long removes overflow up to about 9.2e18. int to double keeps fractions but stops being exact for very large integers. Changing a type to boolean breaks every arithmetic use.
